title: Songs that keep God close
hookLine: a sadhu sings his teacher from head to foot, and the song is still sung after the evening lamps
carry: kirtan: singing god's form keeps him near

cards: A harmonium, a pair of small cymbals, a handful of voices in a mandir after the evening lamps. The song is a kind of portrait.
It moves slowly over one person, the way an eye moves over a face it loves: the forehead, the eyes, the smile, the hands, the feet. The man who first sang it wasn't a painter.
He was a sadhu, one of a circle of poets who traveled with Swaminarayan and turned what they saw into songs. Today, the last day in Gujarat: the poet-sadhus, and the songs they left behind.

teach.b: Tradition remembers several by name. Muktanand Swami, the elder disciple who welcomed Nilkanth at Loj. Premanand Swami, a singer and musician.
Nishkulanand Swami, who also told his teacher's life in the Bhaktachintamani.
Their songs are kirtan, praise sung together, and they're still sung in Swaminarayan mandirs and homes. First, songs of watching.
Tradition says Premanand sang Swaminarayan's form from head to foot, and the shape of his day: how he rose, how he bathed, how he sat with the people who came to see him.
For his followers he is God, Narayan, so these songs are a darshan you can carry: seeing the beloved with your eyes shut.
This is one of bhakti's oldest ways, smarana, remembering. Across Hindu traditions, devotees sing God's form in loving detail, so the heart has something to hold.
Swaminarayan devotees sing these songs at night, so the day ends with God close.
Then, songs of longing, in the voice of a devotee who misses the beloved and can't bear the distance. Longing isn't a failure of faith here. It's part of love, and the poets give it a tune.
Then, songs of letting go. Nishkulanand's verses press on vairagya, detachment. In paraphrase, one says that giving things up doesn't hold unless detachment has reached the heart.
And that's where Gujarat ends: a boy on the road, a name that became a greeting, four things held together, a letter of no harm, a company of the true, and a circle of poets singing God close.

how: Swaminarayan devotees sing kirtans by the tradition's poet-sadhus at mandir gatherings and at home, including songs that describe Swaminarayan's form and his daily life.

games.q: it's late, and a devotee sings of God's face, hands and feet before sleep. by the poet-sadhus' way, what is the singing doing?
o: remembering God's form in love, so he stays close.
keeping a record in case people forget the facts.
filling the quiet until it's time to sleep.
games.why: this is smarana, remembering, through kirtan: the poet-sadhus sang his form and day so devotees could end each day with God near.

practice: Bring to mind someone you love, living or gone, or, if you pray, the form of God you pray to, and let your attention move over them the way the song does: the forehead, the eyes, the smile, the hands, one detail for each breath.
When the mind wanders, come back to the last detail you saw. If missing someone feels heavy today, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Gujarat's Swaminarayan. Today, the poet-sadhus and their kirtan: songs that remember God's form and day, the heart's longing, and letting go. Today's word.

orig.note: a song of praise to God, sung together.

carryVoice: Your line: kirtan, singing God's form keeps him near. A tune can carry a face for a lifetime. Rest well.
